Monday. Vaibhav counted: he had called Indu three times, planned the birthday dinner and booked the table. She had answered with "sure 👍" and nothing else. His jaw tightened. He typed a long message about effort, then deleted it.

The next Sunday, he decided to plan nothing for ten days and simply see what happened. He didn't tell Indu and he didn't sulk. Ten days went by with two memes from her and no plans.

Two Fridays later he called. "I noticed I'm always the one who calls. Is that because it's hard for you, or because you'd rather not?" Indu was quiet, then said her new job left her flat by evening and she'd assumed he liked organising. She offered to plan the next one herself. He said he'd like that, and that he would still call sometimes, just not every time.

qa.q: What did Indu answer when Vaibhav planned the birthday dinner?
qa.a: She answered with "sure" and a thumbs-up, and nothing else.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he deleted his long message, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Resentful. His jaw tightened, and he wrote about effort but did not send it, perhaps to avoid a blurt of anger.

qa.q: Why was it useful for Vaibhav to step back for ten days before speaking?
qa.a: It showed him what happened when he did not organise anything, so he could ask from facts rather than from silent resentment.

qa.q: How did Indu see the pattern before Vaibhav asked?
qa.a: She assumed he liked organising, and her new job left her flat by evening, so she had not realised it felt one-sided to him.

grounding: Vaibhav does all the reaching out, steps back once to see the truth, then speaks honestly and decides what the friendship deserves.

In Thodupuzha, Jeevan was the one who arranged everything: the Onam cricket match, the Sunday tea at Kuttan's shop by the bus stand, the calls whenever Harsha came home from Bengaluru. Two months ago he counted: of the last ten calls, he had made all ten.
He didn't send an angry message. He just decided to wait once, to see.
Three weeks passed. Harsha posted photos from a trek. No call.
Jeevan felt the old resentment rise, then made himself think it through while pruning pepper vines on his uncle's plot. Harsha wasn't cruel; he was busy and careless. Did the friendship still give Jeevan something? Yes. When they did talk, it was easy.
On the fourth Sunday, Jeevan called. "I waited to see if you'd call first. You didn't. It stung a bit." Harsha was quiet, then said, "Sorry, machane. I'm lazy with calls, not with you."
They agreed Harsha would plan the next meet. Jeevan decided a smaller friendship could still be a real one.

qa.q: How many of the last ten calls had Jeevan made?
What did Jeevan feel after three weeks with no call?
qa.a: The old resentment rose; he felt hurt and let down, though he chose to think it through calmly.

qa.q: What was wise about Jeevan's experiment?
qa.a: He stepped back once without an ultimatum, looked honestly at what he saw, then told Harsha calmly how it felt and let Harsha plan the next meet.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the lack of calls?
qa.a: As his own laziness with calls, not a lack of care for Jeevan, and he feels sorry once he hears it stung.

grounding: Shows always being the one who reaches out, stepping back once to see the truth, and deciding what the friendship deserves.

Every month for a year, Diego had booked the table at the taco place near Esther's flat in Mexico City, sent the reminder and paid the deposit. Every month Esther showed up, hugged him, and never once asked about next time.
In October he nearly sent her a long message: "Maybe I'm the only one who cares about this friendship." He saved it in drafts instead and made a quieter plan: this month, he wouldn't book. Just to see.
The first of November came and went. Diego checked his phone more than he wanted to admit.
On the ninth, Esther called. "Hey, did I miss the dinner message? I kept waiting for your reminder. I realised I don't even know how to book that place. That's embarrassing."
Diego laughed despite himself. "You could learn."
"Okay. December is mine. I'm booking somewhere new."
He deleted the draft that night. The answer hadn't been perfect, but it was an answer.

qa.q: Where did Diego book the table every month?
qa.a: At the taco place near Esther's flat in Mexico City.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling when he wrote the long message in October?
qa.a: Resentful and unappreciated, as if he were the only one who cared about the friendship.

qa.q: Why was not booking a better test than sending the draft?
qa.a: It let Diego see the truth without an ultimatum and gave Esther room to step up on her own.

qa.q: How does Esther see her part in the dinners?
qa.a: She realises, embarrassed, that she had simply waited for Diego's reminders, and offers to plan December.

grounding: Illustrates doing all the planning in a friendship and stepping back once, instead of a dramatic ultimatum, to see what is true.
